## Learning Theory, Ensembles, and Structured Inference

This community spans the mathematical foundations, algorithms, and applications of machine learning. Computational and algorithmic learning theory study the design, analysis, and computational limits of learning without or with statistical assumptions; concept classes, Vapnik–Chervonenkis theory, Cover’s theorem, and the bias–variance tradeoff provide key theoretical perspectives. Computational and android epistemology connect learning and inference with knowledge, induction, cognition, and computability.

Core predictive methods include decision trees (ID3-derived C4.5, CHAID, alternating decision trees, CN2 rule induction, and pruning), binary and multilabel classification, classifier chains, and cascading classifiers. Ensemble methods combine weak or multiple experts through boosting (AdaBoost, BrownBoost, CoBoost), bootstrap aggregating, and committee machines.

The community also covers probabilistic and causal systems: Bayesian networks, Chow–Liu trees, kernel regularization interpreted Bayesianly, Bayesian structural time series, causal models, and the causal Markov condition. Semi-supervised methods such as co-training, CoBoost, and Coupled Pattern Learner address limited labeled data and semantic drift.

Current developments emphasize robust learning under adversarial conditions, reliable calibration and cross-validation, causal impact and forecasting, and scalable approximate nearest-neighbor search to address high-dimensionality. Diffusion maps provide nonlinear dimensionality reduction, while NIPS serves as a major venue for ongoing machine-learning research.

## AI: Foundations, Agents, Applications, and Futures

This community spans artificial intelligence’s history, theory, applications, and cultural consequences. Historical landmarks include MIT’s AI Memos, McCarthy’s 1958 *Advice Taker*, the Dartmouth tradition commemorated by AI@50, government programs such as Alvey, and funding reversals associated with ALPAC and AI winters.

Core methods include abductive and temporal reasoning, TBox/ABox knowledge representation, anti-unification, action-model learning, action selection, anticipation, anytime algorithms, and Solomonoff’s algorithmic probability. AIXI combines Solomonoff induction with sequential decision theory as a theoretical reinforcement-learning agent. Agent architectures and communication languages—including FIPA-ACL and KQML—address intelligent-system organization and interaction.

Language technologies feature Apertium’s open-source rule-based machine translation, AppTek’s speech recognition, machine translation, NLP, and machine-learning systems, and challenges characterized as ASR-complete or AI-complete. Applications range from medical diagnosis and scientific discovery to robotics, ambient intelligence, digital libraries, and autonomous vehicles, represented by Alberto Broggi, Anthony Levandowski, and the ACROSS cognitive-robotics project.

Notable systems include 20Q, which guesses thoughts through yes/no questions; AlphaGo, which defeated professional Go players in 2015–16; and AIVA, a deep-learning music composer registered with SACEM in 2016. The community also examines AI’s perceived “effect,” hypothetical takeover scenarios, capability control through AI boxing, and alignment with human goals. Fiction and media, including *.hack* and *A Fire Upon the Deep*, provide cultural perspectives on intelligent systems.

## Stereoscopic 3D Imaging and Entertainment

This community centers on creating, displaying, and perceiving three-dimensional imagery. Core concepts include binocular vision, binocular and cyclodisparity, depth perception, stereopsis, and visual effects such as convergence micropsia. Autostereograms and ASCII stereograms demonstrate single-image depth illusions.

Production methods include paired-camera capture, computer-generated or post-produced 2D-to-3D conversion, and specialized systems such as the Fusion Camera System, 3D camcorders, Fujifilm FinePix Real 3D cameras, and InTru3D animation. Presentation technologies include anaglyph and ColorCode 3-D glasses, active-shutter systems, digital cinema formats, Dolby 3D, IMAX 3D, and Disney Digital 3-D branding. Autostereoscopic approaches—including parallax barriers, eye tracking, integral imaging, HR3D, and holographic displays—seek glasses-free viewing.

Holography records light fields through interference patterns; holographic interference microscopy applies these principles to phase-based microscopic imaging. Major industry participants include IMAX Corporation, 3D Entertainment, 3ality Technica, and Digital Revolution Studios.

Current developments include early standardization of DVB 3D-TV for cable, terrestrial, and satellite transmission, expanding digital cinema and Blu-ray stereoscopic systems, and research into multiscopic, content-adaptive displays. Health research addresses visually induced symptoms and vergence-related effects during 3D viewing.

## Computer Vision, Imaging, and 3D Reconstruction

This community centers on computer vision, image processing, scientific visualization, and three-dimensional graphics. Core topics include 3D modeling, projection, scanning, object recognition, pose estimation, reconstruction from multiple images, and time-varying (4D) reconstruction. Applications span medical imaging, engineering, geospatial surveying, entertainment, augmented reality, biometrics, speech and lip reading, ecological monitoring, and historic preservation.

Key methods include active and passive reconstruction, photogrammetry, affine-invariant feature adaptation, articulated-body and object pose estimation, active vision, and deformable active contours (“snakes”) for segmentation and tracking. Image-enhancement techniques include adaptive histogram equalization, anisotropic (Perona–Malik) diffusion, acutance adjustment, analog processing, and Abel transforms. Automatic image annotation and species identification apply recognition and classification to large image collections.

Important systems include 3D Slicer for medical image analysis; Amira and Avizo for 3D/4D scientific visualization; Aphelion and ANIMAL for image-processing development; 3DF Zephyr for automatically generating models from photographs; and Artec 3D scanners, including the Shapify.me full-body system. Augmented-reality trackers, motion-capture tools, audio-visual speech recognition, and automated lip reading extend vision into interactive and multimodal applications.

Ongoing developments include commercial 3D scanning and photogrammetry, practical depth-sensor systems, UAV-based aerial surveying, and continued research led by figures such as Andrew Blake, Andrew Zisserman, and Anil K. Jain.

## Neural Networks, Learning Methods, and Scalable AI Systems

This community covers foundational machine learning concepts, neural-network architectures, learning algorithms, probabilistic methods, and applied AI systems. Artificial neurons, activation functions, connectionism, ADALINE, the delta rule, and backpropagation establish core models and training principles, while recurrent backpropagation, associative memories, autoencoders, and catastrophic interference address memory, representation, sequential learning, and forgetting.

Deep learning is represented by convolutional neural networks, convolutional deep belief networks, and frameworks such as Apache MXNet, Apache SINGA, Deeplearning4j, and Apache SystemDS. These systems emphasize flexible programming, distributed training, hardware scalability, and integration with Hadoop or Spark. Apache Spark and Giraph provide broader cluster and graph-processing infrastructure.

Other methods include ALOPEX, Bayesian hierarchical modeling and optimization, averaged one-dependence estimators, analogical modeling, decision lists, and apprenticeship learning through inverse reinforcement learning. Cross-entropy and decision boundaries provide statistical and classification foundations.

Applications span acoustic modeling for speech recognition, semantic text analysis, sentiment analysis, image recognition, image captioning, and computer vision. DeepDream explores neural image generation, while Facebook’s Darkforest combines convolutional learning with Monte Carlo tree search for Go. More recent developments include differentiable neural computers, which integrate deep learning with differentiable structured memory, and computational neurogenetic models linking neural, genetic, and brain-function modeling.

Current developments include extensions to process-mining algorithms, enterprise smart-data platforms, increasingly automated text generation, and large-scale behavioral and trend analytics.

## Evolutionary Computation and Adaptive AI

This community centers on evolutionary computation and machine learning, with applications in optimization, program synthesis, neural networks, computer vision, design, and generative art. Evolutionary algorithms use populations of candidate solutions, fitness evaluation, selection, mutation, recombination, and inheritance. Major approaches include genetic programming, gene expression programming, grammatical evolution, differential evolution, estimation of distribution algorithms, extremal optimization, cross-entropy optimization, and evolutionary programming.

Important representations and mechanisms include chromosomes, genetic operators, defining length, fitness functions and effective fitness, cooperative coevolution, cellular evolutionary algorithms, cultural algorithms, and compositional pattern-producing networks. Digital organisms and Darwin machines model variation and selection, while artificial development explores genotype–phenotype mappings. Evolutionary multimodal optimization seeks multiple solutions rather than only one optimum.

Neural-learning topics include backpropagation through time and structure, competitive learning, active learning, grammar induction, and evolutionary acquisition of neural topologies (EANT/EANT2), which evolves both network structures and weights. Evolving intelligent systems extend this direction through online adaptation of model parameters and structure.

Software support includes AForge.NET for vision and AI, and Accord.NET for numerical methods, optimization, statistics, machine learning, neural networks, and signal/image processing. DEAP provides Python tools for rapid evolutionary-computation prototyping, including genetic algorithms, genetic programming, particle swarms, differential evolution, and distribution-based methods.

This community centers on interoperable metadata, controlled vocabularies, semantic Web technologies, and digital-content workflows. Major standards include Dublin Core, AgMES, AGROVOC, EuroVoc, FAST, Darwin Core, and the FAO geopolitical ontology. Current development includes evolving agricultural and biodiversity standards, work-in-progress workflow models, multilingual expansion of EuroVoc and FAO systems, and increasing machine processing of microformats and semantic metadata, including Google’s parsing of hCard, hProduct, and hReview.

## Visual Recognition, Affective Computing, and Intelligent Surveillance

This community covers computer vision methods for modeling, recognizing, and interpreting faces, objects, emotions, and temporal signals. Active Shape Models and Active Appearance Models use landmark-based statistical representations, including point distribution models, to deform toward shapes and jointly match appearance. Eigenfaces apply covariance-derived eigenvectors to face recognition, while elastic matching uses nonlinear image warping. Deep Lambertian Networks combine deep belief networks with Lambertian reflectance assumptions to address illumination variation. Dynamic Time Warping compares sequences that differ in speed and timing, supporting applications such as speech and video analysis.

Face detection locates faces, while facial recognition systems identify or verify people against image databases. The FERET program and FERET database established sponsored research, evaluation procedures, and a large benchmark dataset; the Facial Images National Database linked mugshots and identifying marks with police records.

Affective computing develops systems that recognize, interpret, process, or simulate emotion. Emotion recognition commonly uses facial expressions, and Affectiva applies facial and physiological cues to advertising and political polling.

Surveillance applications include CCTV, AI-based detection of people, vehicles, objects, and restricted-area intrusions, and automatic number-plate recognition. UK ANPR operates across about 8,500 cameras, generating 25–35 million daily reads. INDECT represents EU-funded research into automated threat and abnormal-behavior detection from CCTV streams.

This community centers on computational models for language, sequential data, and biological inference. Finite-state methods include deterministic and nondeterministic finite automata, alternating, Büchi and co-Büchi automata, generalized automata, aperiodic automata, and DFA minimization. Forward, forward–backward, Baum–Welch, and expectation–maximization algorithms enable filtering, smoothing, parameter estimation, and latent-variable learning. fMLLR adapts HMM-based speech recognition, with HTK providing a major HMM toolkit. Dependability state models apply Markov chains to reliability analysis.

Natural-language applications include activity recognition, word alignment and IBM statistical translation models, sense-tagged corpus acquisition, Brown clustering, Brill transformation-based tagging, and recursive-transition-network parsing. Gene prediction uses statistical models such as GLIMMER’s interpolated Markov models. Folding@home applies distributed computing to protein folding and drug design, while eye tracking supports behavioral and interface research.

Developments include ANS compression, open-source finite-state tooling, and modern optimization replacing GIS/IIS; FreeHAL is no longer active.

## AI-Enabled Decision Management and Information Services

This community centers on rule-based artificial intelligence, decision management, predictive analytics, and commercial information services.

Business rule management systems (BRMS) define, deploy, execute, monitor, and maintain operational policies separately from application code. Business rules engines execute rules over facts, priorities, and conditions, while event–condition–action (ECA) rules connect triggering events to logical tests and actions. Conflict-resolution strategies select among simultaneously applicable production rules. Backward chaining reasons from goals; forward and backward inference are supported by systems such as Drools, whose production-rule engine uses an enhanced Rete algorithm and is part of the broader KIE technology umbrella. CLIPS provides a public-domain expert-system shell, while FuzzyCLIPS adds exact, fuzzy, and combined reasoning. d3web supports diagnostic trees, heuristic rules, set-covering models, and flowcharts. Cleverpath AION and InRule are additional expert-system or BRMS offerings, and SAP’s BRFplus integrates business rules with NetWeaver and web services.

Decision Model and Notation (DMN) standardizes readable, interoperable decision models for business and IT. CRISP-DM describes common data-mining practice.

The community also includes predictive analytics and large-scale data brokers and credit-information firms, including Angoss, CoreLogic (now Cotality), Dun & Bradstreet, Equifax, Experian, FICO, Bread Financial, and Intelius. Developments include ownership changes, corporate rebranding, cloud/service integration, and expanded analytics for credit, fraud, identity, marketing, property, and risk.

This community covers the industrial machine-vision ecosystem, including trade organizations, robotics, camera interfaces, software APIs, and commercial suppliers. GenICam provides a generic programming interface that separates application software from camera-interface technologies such as GigE Vision and Camera Link. Its GenApi and GenTL modules were ratified in 2006 and 2008, respectively.

## Digital Imaging Calibration and Subtraction

This community covers methods for correcting sensor and optical artifacts, reducing noise, and detecting image changes in digital imaging systems.

Key concepts include **fixed-pattern noise (FPN)**—temporally constant pixel-to-pixel non-uniformity, such as hot and cold pixels—and calibration images used to characterize it. A **bias frame** records unwanted electronic signal without exposure, while a **dark frame** records sensor noise, including dark current and fixed-pattern components, during an exposure with the shutter closed. **Dark-frame subtraction** uses this reference to reduce long-exposure noise.

**Correlated double sampling (CDS)** measures a sensor output in a known and an unknown condition, subtracting the first from the second to remove offsets. **Flat-field correction** compensates for variations in pixel sensitivity and optical effects such as vignetting.

More generally, **image subtraction** subtracts pixel or image values to level uneven illumination or identify changes and movement. These techniques are used across digital cameras, scientific detectors, astrophotography, and large telescopes. Current applications highlighted by the articles include computerized searches for moving objects such as asteroids and Kuiper belt objects, alongside routine calibration from consumer cameras to astronomical instruments.

This community concerns bodies of knowledge (BOKs): structured collections of concepts, terms, activities, and skills that define a professional domain and guide practitioners’ work. ## Machine Translation Methods, Tools, and Projects

This community covers major approaches to machine translation (MT), including dictionary-based, example-based, interlingual, interactive, and hybrid systems. Dictionary-based MT translates through lexical entries, optionally using morphological analysis or lemmatisation, and is particularly suited to lists and simple catalogues. Example-based MT uses bilingual parallel corpora and translation by analogy. Interlingual MT converts source text into an abstract, language-independent representation before generating the target language; Distributed Language Translation (DLT) applied this two-stage model through Esperanto as an intermediate language, supporting twelve European languages and networked workstations.

Hybrid MT combines multiple approaches because no single technique consistently provides satisfactory accuracy. Interactive MT instead supports human translators by repeatedly predicting text and revising predictions from user feedback.

Systems and services include Caitra, an Edinburgh-developed online computer-assisted translation tool using AJAX, Ruby on Rails, C++, and the Moses decoder to suggest translations; and Internettolken, an online Swedish service that expanded from English–Swedish to 14 languages and over 120 language combinations. European research projects EuroMatrix (2006–2009) and EuroMatrixPlus (2009–2012) developed MT between EU languages. The community also includes computational linguist Hans Uszkoreit, associated with major academic and AI-centered MT research.

## Digital Imaging Calibration and Subtraction

This community covers methods for correcting sensor and optical artifacts, reducing noise, and detecting image changes in digital imaging systems.

Key concepts include **fixed-pattern noise (FPN)**—temporally constant pixel-to-pixel non-uniformity, such as hot and cold pixels—and calibration images used to characterize it. A **bias frame** records unwanted electronic signal without exposure, while a **dark frame** records sensor noise, including dark current and fixed-pattern components, during an exposure with the shutter closed. **Dark-frame subtraction** uses this reference to reduce long-exposure noise.

**Correlated double sampling (CDS)** measures a sensor output in a known and an unknown condition, subtracting the first from the second to remove offsets. **Flat-field correction** compensates for variations in pixel sensitivity and optical effects such as vignetting.

More generally, **image subtraction** subtracts pixel or image values to level uneven illumination or identify changes and movement. These techniques are used across digital cameras, scientific detectors, astrophotography, and large telescopes. Current applications highlighted by the articles include computerized searches for moving objects such as asteroids and Kuiper belt objects, alongside routine calibration from consumer cameras to astronomical instruments.

## Blockmodeling and Network Analysis

This community centers on blockmodeling, a framework for analyzing social structure by clustering network nodes according to recurring interconnection patterns. It encompasses exploratory (inductive) blockmodeling, which generates hypotheses by defining permitted block types and cluster numbers, and confirmatory (deductive) blockmodeling, which fits networks to a prespecified or partially prespecified blockmodel.

Generalized blockmodeling, introduced in 1994 by Patrick Doreian, Vladimir Batagelj, and Anuška Ferligoj, translates equivalence types into permitted block types through a direct approach. Deterministic blockmodeling uses exact or approximate algorithms and objective functions to minimize discrepancies from ideal structures, without assuming a probabilistic model. Generalized blockmodeling of binary networks evaluates inconsistencies against binary ideal blocks, while valued-network blockmodeling addresses non-binary ties. Homogeneity blockmodeling emphasizes equal tie strengths within blocks, and implicit blockmodeling adds normalization and replaces relevant link parameters with block maxima.

Generalized multilevel blockmodeling extends analysis to linked networks, jointly clustering nodes across sets and connected one-mode and two-mode networks. Software development includes the R package for generalized blockmodeling (2020). The community also includes Andrej Mrvar, known for network analysis and data processing, and Harrison White, whose mathematical models of social structure include blockmodeling and whose work influenced social-network sociology.
